summary: Defines an IMAP4 extension that lets access control lists for mailboxes be manipulated through the IMAP protocol. It was replaced by RFC 4314.

plainLanguage.summary: It lets you say who may open which mailbox, using the same tool you already use for email.

questions: how to share an imap mailbox
how do i grant imap permissions
subtitle: Control who can access shared mailboxes through IMAP.

tldr.problem: Email users need to share mailboxes with colleagues, but IMAP had no way to specify who can do what with a mailbox (read it, add messages, delete messages, or manage permissions). Each implementation had different ad-hoc solutions.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2086 adds five new IMAP commands to manage access control lists: SETACL (grant or revoke rights), DELETEACL (remove an ACL entry), GETACL (list who has access), LISTRIGHTS (show what rights can be granted to someone), and MYRIGHTS (show your own rights). Each entry pairs an identifier (user or group) with a set of single-letter rights.
tldr.outcome: Shared mailboxes can now be configured through IMAP itself, letting users control permissions without command-line administration. It was refined by RFC 4314, which is now the standard.

facts.label: Standard rights codes
facts.value: 9 single-letter codes (l, r, s, w, i, p, c, d, a)

facts.label: Negative rights
facts.value: Prefix identifier with - to remove rights

today: RFC 2086 was obsoleted by RFC 4314, which is now the standard for IMAP4 access control. RFC 4314 refines the mechanism and adds more flexibility for rights handling. ACL remains a widely supported IMAP extension.

sections.title: Shared Mailboxes in IMAP
sections.content:
IMAP is a protocol for managing email, but it had no standard way to control who can access which mailboxes. Organizations often need shared mailboxes--folders that multiple people can access, such as a customer support inbox or a department mailbox. Without access control, administrators had to use system-level commands, and users had no way to manage permissions themselves.

RFC 2086 adds an ACL extension to IMAP that lets access control be managed through the same protocol used for reading mail. An ACL (access control list) is a set of entries, each specifying what a user or group can do with a mailbox.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes multiple people need to use the same email folder. This RFC lets you say which people can use it and what they can do: read messages, add messages, delete messages, or change the permissions.

sections.title: Identifiers and Rights
sections.content:
Each ACL entry pairs an identifier with a set of rights. An identifier is a user name, a group name, or the special identifier anyone (meaning all users, including unauthenticated ones). Identifiers starting with a dash (for example, -fred) represent negative rights: they remove permissions from a user instead of granting them.

Rights are single-letter codes that control what operations are allowed: l for lookup (mailbox visible in LIST/LSUB), r for read (SELECT and FETCH), s for seen status, w for write (store flags), i for insert (APPEND/COPY), p for post (send to submission address), c for create (sub-mailboxes), d for delete (EXPUNGE), and a for administer (change ACL).

An implementation may tie certain rights together; for example, granting the write right might automatically include the seen right. Clients can query which rights can be granted using the LISTRIGHTS command.
sections.plainLanguage: The ACL lists users and what they can do. A user can read, write, delete, create folders, or manage permissions. Different systems may tie some rights together, so if you can write, you might automatically be able to mark messages as seen.

sections.title: ACL Commands
sections.content:
The ACL extension adds five new commands to IMAP:

SETACL (mailbox identifier rights): Grants or revokes permissions. The rights string may start with a plus sign (add rights), a minus sign (remove rights), or neither (replace all rights). For example, SETACL INBOX bob +ri grants bob read and insert rights, while SETACL INBOX bob minus d revokes delete rights.

DELETEACL (mailbox identifier): Removes all permissions for an identifier from a mailbox's ACL.

GETACL (mailbox): Returns the entire ACL for a mailbox, listing all identifier and rights pairs.

LISTRIGHTS (mailbox identifier): Tells what rights could be granted to an identifier. Some systems may force certain rights together or prohibit granting certain rights. The response includes required rights (always granted) and optional rights (may or may not be granted).

MYRIGHTS (mailbox): Returns the set of rights the logged-in user has for that mailbox.
sections.plainLanguage: You can add or remove permissions with SETACL, delete all permissions with DELETEACL, see who has access with GETACL, ask what permissions are possible with LISTRIGHTS, and check your own permissions with MYRIGHTS.

sections.title: Security and Access Control
sections.content:
Access control lists only work if the IMAP server enforces them correctly. A crucial security requirement is that ACL commands must not leak information. For example, a GETACL command on a mailbox the user does not have permission to access should not reveal the ACL or even admit the mailbox exists. The server must treat lack of access as if the mailbox does not exist.

The anyone identifier applies to all users, including unauthenticated ones. Implementations must be careful not to grant dangerous rights (like delete or administer) to anyone unless intended.

Implementers have flexibility in how they combine rights from multiple ACL entries that apply to a user. Some systems union the rights; others use the most specific matching entry. Clients cannot assume a particular strategy and should verify permissions using MYRIGHTS.
sections.plainLanguage: The system must not let you see who has access to a folder you cannot access yourself. If you grant permission to anyone, all users (even unauthenticated ones) get it, so be careful.

items.label: Lookup
items.desc: Mailbox is visible in LIST and LSUB commands.

items.label: Read
items.desc: Can SELECT mailbox and FETCH messages.

items.label: Seen
items.desc: Can store SEEN flag across sessions.

items.label: Write
items.desc: Can store flags other than SEEN and DELETED.

items.label: Insert
items.desc: Can APPEND or COPY messages into mailbox.

items.label: Post
items.desc: Can send mail to mailbox submission address.

items.label: Delete
items.desc: Can store DELETED flag and EXPUNGE.

items.label: Administer
items.desc: Can run SETACL to change ACL.
